Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League match between Crystal Palace and Liverpool at Selhurst Park.

The pressure is building on Palace head coach Pierre Sage, who desperately needs a win to lift the mood and propel the club out of the relegation zone. Nottingham Forest’s impressive 3-1 win over Manchester City on Saturday evening means that Palace have dropped to a lowly 19th and are two points from safety. To make matters worse, Sage’s beleaguered side have also conceded the most goals in the division (21 in nine games).

On Thursday night, Daichi Kamada’s stoppage-time equaliser rescued a 1-1 home draw in the Europa League against Hoffenheim, after Palace delivered an alarmingly lacklustre performance.

Meanwhile, Liverpool also endured midweek European torment, as Andoni Iraola’s men fell to an error-ridden 3-2 defeat away at Fenerbahce in the Champions League, having previously lost 1-0 to Arsenal in their most recent Premier League encounter on Merseyside last weekend, which has left the club in sixth but just five points behind second-place Man City.

Speaking to reporters on Friday, Iraola said: “I think that’s the challenge, especially in a club like Liverpool. One week ago in this same press conference, we were on a run, everything was in a good place and we were in a better mood. And now, two defeats, it changes. It has to change and it has to be like this in a club like ours. Now we have to react after two defeats.”

As for Palace’s team news, Jean-Philippe Mateta is serving the first match of a three-game domestic ban after he was sent off for Palace in the 2-0 defeat to Tottenham last time out in the league. Liverpool’s long-term absentees include Hugo Ekitike, Giovanni Leoni, Conor Bradley and Jeremie Frimpong, while Ryan Gravenberch could also miss out after struggling with a heel injury.

Kick-off is at 14:00, with team news arriving shortly.

#1010. Rights court rules Turkey must release jailed lawmaker Atalay

The European Court of Human Rights has called for the release of imprisoned elected lawmaker Can Atalay. Atalay has been in prison for almost five years despite rulings from the Turkish Constitutional Court.

The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) ruled against Turkey over the detention of human rights lawyer and elected lawmaker Can Atalay.

The ECHR published its decision on Tuesday, saying that Turkey must release Atalay and allow him to take up his seat in the Turkish parliament.

The court ruled that his continued detention had been intended to silence him and undermine political pluralism.

It ordered Turkey to pay him €32,500 (about $35,700) in compensation.

The judges stressed that Atalay's case should not be considered separately, but rather in the wider context of the detention of political opponents, human rights activists and journalists in Turkey.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Turkey was among the original signatories of the European Convention on Human Rights. Yet it has previously refused to comply with the court's decisions in the cases of rights activist Osman Kavala and prominent Kurdish politician Selahattin Demirtas.

As a lawyer, Atalay represented victims in numerous social and political cases in Turkey, as well as in freedom of speech cases involving journalists and writers.

He was also among the leading voices in the 2013 Gezi protests, which the government called an attempted coup.

Because of his involvement in the protests, Atalay, along with seven others, was sentenced to 18 years in prison in April 2022 for "aiding and abetting an attempted coup."

Continuing his struggle from the infamous Silivri prison, Atalay ran as a candidate for the Workers' Party of Turkey (TIP) in the 2023 parliamentary elections.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A candidate for the earthquake-hit province of Hatay, he won his seat but was denied release despite multiple rulings by the Constitutional Court, Turkey's top court.

His parliamentary status was revoked in 2024, a decision the Constitutional Court later overturned. President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's party stopped the opposition from formally reading the decision in parliament.

Although a year later an opposition lawmaker read the decision in parliament, Atalay remains in jail.

After the ECHR's ruling was published, TIP leader Erkan Bas took to social media to call for Atalay's release and the restoration of his parliamentary mandate.

#1009. Joshua Kimmich takes on Bayern Munich over 'unacceptable' treatment of Jamal Musiala: Club captain hits out at chiefs after they publicly undermined youngster following his health diagnosis

Published: 03:16 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 06:39 EST, 26 November 2026

Joshua Kimmich has hammered his own club Bayern Munich for their 'incomprehensible' and 'unacceptable' undermining of Jamal Musiala's ongoing illness battle.

Musiala, the 23-year-old golden boy of German football, has hardly played this season due to seizures brought on by 'neurological dysfunction' and has an £18m-a-year salary until 2030.

Last week, Bayern board member Karl-Heinz Rummenigge suggested the club could discuss him taking a pay cut, arguing: 'We need to talk to the family, the player, and the agency, because then these sums of money, sorry, with all due respect, are no longer feasible.

‘I cannot imagine that Jamal wants to leave the club or that any other club would buy him under these conditions.'

There was a huge outcry after Rummenigge's remarks, with the likes of Jude Bellingham, Michael Olise and Rio Ferdinand all backing Musiala.

And when asked about the situation after Bayern's 2-1 defeat by Lille in the Champions League on Wednesday night, Kimmich said: 'What happened now is something that simply must never happen in this way. I find it completely incomprehensible.

Joshua Kimmich hammered Bayern Munich for their handling of Jamal Musiala's situation

Musiala came off the bench for Bayern in their 2-1 defeat by Lille on Wednesday night

'I think this is something that should be discussed behind closed doors, something you can address with Jamal's agent or with Jamal himself. And I think the other side is open to that as well.

'I believe I've also read that they've met and are supposed to issue a statement. What I don't understand is the way this is being communicated publicly. It must never happen that a player is made to bear the brunt of it.

'Of course, the club always comes first and is bigger than us as players, but it's not bigger than the person. And that's an absolute no-go. It's also not the Bayern way. Especially at this particular time, when I've often emphasised how special this club is.

'Even in my own situation, the club was incredibly special. You could really feel that this sense of togetherness was being lived out.'

Kimmich pointed out that Musiala's health issues are in no way a result of him being unprofessional.

'We mustn't forget that he underwent another operation in the summer and then suffered another injury afterwards,' he continued.

'But I see him and spend time with him every day. I see how he works and how hard he works. That's another important aspect of the situation. It's not as though he's having problems because he's unprofessional. Quite the opposite: he's here every day, naturally wants to get the very best out of himself, works extremely hard every day and, I think, genuinely enjoys being part of our team.

'I hope he knows that all of us are 100% behind him, both the team and the club officials.'

While Kimmich offered his support to Musiala, he admitted he did understand the difficulty the club faces financially with one of their most expensive players unable to start more than one Bundesliga game this season.

Musiala collapsed on the pitch at two consecutive games in August (pictured being helped by team-mates against RB Leipzig)

He continued: 'Generally speaking, you have to look at the situation from different perspectives. I have absolute understanding for the fact that this is not an easy situation for a club either.

'Of course, I've witnessed Jamal's journey over the past two years. I mean, he carried us at the Euros and was our standout player afterwards. Then he signed a contract extension, was given the number 10 shirt here and with the German national team. Then came the first muscle injury. I can speak from personal experience: when you extend your contract, especially at that age, it's not about sitting back and enjoying the next five years.

'Rather, it's a source of motivation and a responsibility you want to live up to. Then Jamal had the illness and the serious injury. We mustn't forget that over the past year and a half, I don't think he's managed to play four or five games in a row.

'So it's understandable to some extent that he's not performing at his usual level. And it's also understandable that the club might be concerned because of the illness.'

The Germany international was diagnosed over the summer with absence seizures, a form of epilepsy which causes 'brief but easily treatable seizures'.

Musiala shocked the sporting world when he collapsed in two matches earlier this season, with Bayern manager Vincent Kompany explaining that the player had suffered from a reaction to a change in his medication.

Honorary president Uli Hoeness was the first to speak out on the potential drop-off in form Musiala might suffer with long-term absences, claiming earlier this month that he 'may never regain the performance level he once had'.

'We are facing a dilemma in this case, as he is suffering from an illness that cannot simply be cured, but it can be controlled to a certain extent with the use of medication,' Hoeness told German outlet BR24.

Both Uli Hoeness and Karl-Heinz Rummenigge have made comments suggesting consequences should Musiala not return to his level

Chief executive Jan-Christian Dreesen then backed up Hoeness's comments and implied that Musiala's contract may need to be 'assessed'.

'We're monitoring his level of play. He'll certainly need time to improve further – like any injured player,' Dreesen said in discussion with AZ. 'And then we need to calmly assess the situation and, if necessary, sit down with his family and management.

'Either we'll all be happy together and he'll be the same Jamal he always was – or, if he's a different Jamal along the way, we'll have to discuss it.'

'If we're not consistently at a level that also aligns with the economic realities, then we'll have to talk to each other. Nevertheless, we have a valid contract, and that's the end of it.'

The 23-year-old is one of Bayern's highest-earners, having signed a deal with the club to extend his time in Bavaria in February 2025.

Adding fuel to the fire days later was former CEO Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, who told Sky Sports/RTL that he thought it was almost reasonable to discuss a renegotiation should Musiala not return to the level at which he once played.

But the player union Fifpro were forthright in their disagreement with his statements,  releasing a statement claiming that all parties currently sharing their views on Musiala's contract 'should know better'.

'Bayern's honorary president, chief executive and former chief executive have all publicly questioned Musiala's contract in quick succession,' the statement read.

'In Fifpro's view, this is a co-ordinated strategy to put pressure on Musiala and his representatives ahead of any negotiations. A club of Bayern's standing should know better.'

When this statement was shared to social media via journalist Fabrizio Romano, global talents including Jude Bellingham and Musiala's team-mate Michael Olise were among those to like the post.

Criticisms were even more fiery in Germany, with the vice president of Germany's player union Michael Franz accusing the club of harassment.

'What the Bayern Munich officials are doing, and I don't mean Kompany and (Max) Eberl (director of sport), who have behaved impeccably, seems despicable to me,' Franz shared in an interview with Sport1. 'There is even something about it that resembles harassment.'

'A footballer's level of performance can be discussed publicly, but it is not right to talk about his illness and the salary he receives in such circumstances. We must not forget that Jamal Musiala has done everything in his power to come back.'

'Money has become more important than the person, and that is unacceptable.'

Musiala collapsed twice within four days in mid-August, first during Bayern's match against Leipzig – shortly after scoring – and then against Heidenheim.

#1003. Back to 1997: Russia wants NATO to roll back its eastern expansion

The Kremlin is reportedly calling on NATO to withdraw from large parts of Eastern Europe. What this would mean for the security of millions of Europeans — and what lies behind Russia's plan.

During talks on ending the war in Ukraine, Russian representatives in Abu Dhabi presented a document containing far-reaching demands, The New York Times reports.

Dated November 10, the document reportedly calls not only for an end to Western arms deliveries to Ukraine but also for NATO to withdraw its troops and bases and move them back to where they were in 1997.

The year 1997 refers to the NATO alliance before its first eastward expansion, according to the Kremlin. At the time, NATO had 16 members. Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary had already been invited to join but did not formally become members of the defense alliance until two years later. In the following years, more countries in Central, Eastern and Southeastern Europe joined, followed most recently by countries in Scandinavia. Today, NATO has 32 member states in Europe and North America.

According to the report, Russia is not explicitly demanding that Central and Eastern European countries leave, but rather that the NATO alliance end its military presence in those countries.

A withdrawal of NATO troops and bases from member states that joined the alliance after 1997 would significantly weaken their defense capabilities. For example, since 2004, NATO allies, including Germany, have taken turns policing the airspace over Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.

Because the Baltic states do not have fighter jets of their own for independent air policing, NATO provides the capability. Since 2026, the mission has been part of a broader air defense presence. The planned deployment of the German Lithuania Brigade, which is expected to be fully operational by the end of 2027, would also have to be halted.

In Romania, meanwhile, the Mihail Kogalniceanu Air Base near Constanța on the Black Sea is currently being expanded. Once completed, it is set to become Europe's largest NATO air base by area — even larger than Ramstein in Germany.

"Under no circumstances will we allow anyone to establish new security rules for this part of the world over the heads of Poland and Europe," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told TVP World. His Bulgarian counterpart, Rumen Radev, called a NATO withdrawal "unthinkable and unrealistic." No country should be forced by external pressure to reverse its decision on which alliance to join.

Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal also rejected any Russian say in changes to Europe's security order: "We have nothing to discuss with Russia about Europe's security order; it is working well."

The strong rejection from the capitals of NATO's eastern members, however, masks fears along the alliance's eastern flank that a deal between Washington and Moscow could turn their security into a bargaining chip.

In the event of an armed attack on a NATO member, the other alliance members are obligated under Article 5 to come to its aid. Each member decides for itself what measures it considers necessary, which may include the use of military force.

For the mutual defense commitment to deter a potential aggressor, that country must believe NATO can intervene militarily quickly and effectively in a crisis. The deployment of allied troops along the eastern flank serves precisely this purpose. A withdrawal would make defense more difficult and could lead Russia to believe that an attack on NATO territory would involve fewer risks for Moscow.

As part of their security framework, European countries have agreed that states are free to decide which alliances they wish to join. NATO points to Article 10 of its founding treaty, which enshrines its open-door policy for European countries. The 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act also explicitly stated that neither side had the right to veto the other's decisions.

Back in November 1990, the participating states of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe (CSCE), including the Soviet Union, had already agreed in the Charter of Paris to respect each country's freedom to choose its own security arrangements.

During the negotiations surrounding German reunification, then-US Secretary of State James Baker and German Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher used language that suggested putting limits on NATO's eastward expansion.

Their remarks came during discussions about unified Germany's membership in NATO and the possible deployment of NATO forces on the territory of the former East Germany. However, no written, legally binding general promise was ever agreed that NATO would never expand to include other former Warsaw Pact countries.

In the 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act, both sides declared that they no longer considered each other adversaries. NATO stated that, under the security conditions prevailing at the time and in the foreseeable future, it intended to ensure its collective defense through reinforcement rather than the additional permanent stationing of "substantial combat forces." The agreement explicitly gave Moscow no veto over NATO decisions.

In the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, Russia, the United States and the United Kingdom reaffirmed their commitment to respect Ukraine's independence and existing borders and to refrain from the use of force. These assurances were linked to Ukraine's decision to give up its nuclear weapons. However, the memorandum did not oblige the United States or the United Kingdom to defend Ukraine militarily in the event of an attack. NATO membership was not addressed at the time.

Just over two months before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Kremlin presented two draft treaties to the United States and NATO. In them, Russia demanded an end to further NATO enlargement. The draft agreement with NATO also proposed that Russia and NATO members that had already joined the alliance as of May 27, 1997, refrain from deploying additional troops or weapons on the territory of other European countries beyond the levels stationed there on that date.

Security guarantees for the postwar period and a future security framework for Europe were also on the agenda in Abu Dhabi. Negotiating NATO troop deployments and alliance enlargement alongside an end to the war in Ukraine would give Moscow additional leverage. Russia has long maintained that the "root causes" of the war must be addressed. The Kremlin includes NATO enlargement and the alliance's military presence in Eastern Europe among those causes.

So far, no significant Western player has expressed willingness to accept Russia's demands in Abu Dhabi. On the contrary, former Polish intelligence coordinator Stanislaw Zaryn viewed the talks as an attempt to buy time and weaken the West ahead of another confrontation.

This article was originally published in German.

#997. Dengue has exploded globally with shocking speed

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

A pregnant person with dengue speaks to a nurse in Peru, which has been hit by a surge of cases this year. Credit: Juan Carlos Cisneros/AFP/Getty

The debilitating viral disease called dengue has exploded in incidence far more than previously thought, a new analysis suggests.

The number of reported global cases of dengue, which is transmitted by infected mosquitoes, rose from 430,000 in 1990 to 14.7 million in 2024 — a 34-fold increase, the analysis says.

Dengue is spreading in Europe: how worried should we be?

Dengue is spreading in Europe: how worried should we be?

The data were presented on 22 November at the annual meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene (ASTMH) in National Harbor, Maryland. Scientists also provided some of the strongest results yet about a counter-intuitive way to curb the disease’s staggering spread: the release of specially modified mosquitoes. But researchers also presented discouraging data on other solutions, and scientists at the meeting emphasized that the campaign to beat back dengue will be complicated and costly.

“We’re in an extraordinary and pivotal moment” in the history of studying mosquito-borne illnesses, said Albert Ko, president of ASTMH. Trial results presented at the meeting showed, he said, that “we can get rigorous evidence on what works, what doesn’t and what needs to be done to scale these effective interventions to protect the 4 billion people” around the world who are exposed to dengue and other mosquito-borne illnesses.

Dengue causes fever, headaches and severe bone pain. It is transmitted mainly by Aedes aegypti, a species of mosquito that thrives in warm, urban environments. Global warming and increased urbanization have expanded the mosquitoes’ range. Existing vaccines provide imperfect protection.

Cases of dengue are often recorded in disparate databases that aren’t easily comparable, says Ahyoung Lim, an infectious-disease modeler at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, who was involved in the study on dengue incidence. The results have also been published as a preprint1 on Research Square ahead of peer review. This has meant that no single database has captured the total number of reported dengue cases over time, leading Lim and her team to compile the most complete record of reported cases and use statistical modelling tools to fill in gaps in which data were missing.

The staggering increase in reported cases isn’t surprising, says Eng Eong Ooi, a dengue virologist at Duke–NUS Medical School in Singapore, who was not involved in the research. Populations in urban environments around the world are steadily increasing, he says, which means that “more and more people are living at risk of dengue each year”.

One promising approach to curb dengue starts with breeding mosquitoes and deliberately infecting them with a bacterium called Wolbachia that reduces the insects’ ability to transmit viruses. When released into the wild, these infected mosquitoes pass the bacterium on to their offspring, eventually lowering the number of highly transmissive mosquitoes.

This is the world’s largest ‘mosquito factory’: its goal is to stop dengue

This is the world’s largest ‘mosquito factory’: its goal is to stop dengue

At the ASTMH meeting, another team of researchers shared results from the first randomized controlled trial in the Americas to test Wolbachia’s effect on dengue transmission. Between January 2021 and May 2022, the researchers released roughly 32 million Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes across designated regions of Brazil and monitored almost 6,000 children living inside and outside these regions. The children provided annual blood samples between 2020 and 2024, and the reseachers found that those in the Wolbachia regions were 68% less likely to be infected with dengue compared with those in non-Wolbachia regions.

These positive results mark an important milestone in proving Wolbachia’s potential to drastically reduce dengue cases, says Elisabeth Nelson, an epidemiologist at the Yale School of Public Health in New Haven, Connecticut, and a researcher on the trial.

#994. 'We have players who have been here for four years and can't speak English': Nottingham Forest boss Oliver Glasner slams stars for failing to adapt in England in press conference rant

Published: 04:12 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 07:31 EST, 26 November 2026

Oliver Glasner has criticised Nottingham Forest players that cannot speak English after being in the country for several years, as he called for higher standards at the club.

Forest are currently outside the Premier League relegation zone on goal difference after 11 matches, having won just twice in the top flight since Glasner's arrival in the summer.

Speaking ahead of their Friday night clash against Chelsea, Glasner highlighted the failure of some of his squad to learn English to illustrate how standards needed to rise at the club.

'Stability in a company is having standards,' Glasner said. 'Everybody who joins commits to the standards. I think, very honestly, the standards were not high enough.

'We have players who are here for four years, can't speak English. If you go to Italy, after three months, every player gives his interview in the Italian language.

'For me, if I want to manage in England, I have to speak English. If I want to manage in Italy, I have to speak Italian.

Nottingham Forest boss Oliver Glasner has criticised stars for failing to speak English years after joining the club

Glasner highlighted the issue as an example as he insisted standards need to rise at the club

'Otherwise, Oliver Glasner, if you want to speak in your dialect, stay at home in Austria, everybody understands you, but nowhere else.'

Football clubs regularly enlist the services of language experts in an effort to help foreign stars to settle and communicate with their team-mates.

West Brom and Wolves have worked with Language Partners for around 20 years, with the company providing tailored classes to players and coaches, offering specific skills required for their role at the clubs.

Another company, Communicate Well, has worked with Premier League clubs since 1999, with lessons taking place at training grounds, players’ homes and ‘out and about’ to provide real-life tasks in English.

Chelsea goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez previously revealed Arsenal had included a £20,000 bonus in his first contract with the club, which would be paid when he passed the English proficiency test.

Martinez, who signed for Arsenal in the summer of 2010 from Argentine side Independiente, had reportedly passed the test before Christmas.

English stars moving abroad have received praise in recent years for their efforts to learn the native language, with Jude Bellingham, Anthony Gordon and Trent Alexander-Arnold having all made efforts to become fluent in Spanish.

Alexander-Arnold revealed he had worked with a Spanish tutor for five months prior to joining Real Madrid. The tutor revealed he had started ‘from zero’ but worked every day to be able to speak Spanish at his unveiling at the club.

After speaking Spanish at his Barcelona unveiling, Gordon explained he had initially begun learning the language at Everton when working under Rafael Benitez. He later spoke Spanish with a physio at Newcastle as he targeted a move to Barcelona, while the winger also underwent six formal lessons.

Joao Gomes is among Wolves' foreign imports to have worked with a specialist language company to help them settle at the club

Arsenal put a bonus in Emiliano Martinez's contract to encourage him to learn English

Trent Alexander-Arnold worked with a Spanish tutor for five months before his move to Real Madrid

Daily Mail Sport reported last month that Glasner had not been happy with some of his players' attitudes and their response to his work since joining the club from Crystal Palace in the summer.

Glasner had explosively hit out at his players after their 2-0 defeat at Brentford at the end of October, with the Austrian having warned players either had to buy into his methods to see a turnaround in form or they would have a sixth manager since the start of last season.

The 52-year-old's warning appeared to have been met with a positive response as Forest earned a stunning 3-1 victory over Man City before the international break, but they returned with a 2-0 loss at Bournemouth last weekend.

Glasner had maintained that his squad will have to work hard and show commitment both on and off the pitch to improve.

'We always try to support the players to get the best version of themselves that they can be. But at the end, the players that have to do it, they have to buy in, they have to listen and work hard on the pitch,' Glasner said.

'There is no other opportunity to improve, it would be easy laying on the sofa and doing nothing and you become a better football player or suddenly speak a language all of a sudden.

'It just doesn't work. It is all about how hard you work and how committed you are.

Glasner has insisted his squad need to work hard and show commitment to improve

'I believe none of our players have reached his personal ceilings so far, there is always bits to improve – physically, mentally, technically, tactically – there is always space to improve.

'The most important thing is that players want to improve, then it can happen.'

Glasner met with Forest owner Evangelos Marinakis in London earlier this week, where plans for the January transfer window were discussed.

Forest are expected to target adding around five players to their squad in the window as they bid to turn around their fortunes.

'He was asking "what do you need, what do you want here to improve in the squad, the staff and the environment",' Glasner said.

'He wants the best for Nottingham Forest, he wants the best for everyone here.

'We need to improve in the squad, in the staff, in the environment and this is our discussion. It was a fantastic meeting and it was worth spending six hours travelling.'

Forest face a Chelsea side on Friday that have lost three of their last four league matches.

Glasner’s side will then begin December with matches against Hull, Brighton and Sunderland as they bid to climb the table.

#992. Chelsea bullied by Brian Brobbey and Sunderland

Talk about cramming everything in. Brian Brobbey only played for 67 minutes but, in that time, he collected a yellow card, ripped Levi Colwill’s shirt and earned himself a standing ovation after morphing into a battering ram.

Régis Le Bris, Sunderland’s head coach, said there was nobody like the Netherlands striker in the Premier League and it said everything that everyone wanted to make Brobbey centre of attention after a long overdue home win, even though he had not scored. Everyone, that is, bar Xabi Alonso.

“No, he’s not unstoppable,” Chelsea’s head coach replied when asked why his team had found Brobbey too much to handle. “He’s stoppable – but only when you defend better than we did. We were not bullied. We didn’t produce enough.”

That is one way of putting it. Another would be to say Brobbey was everything that Chelsea, much to Alonso’s disgust, were not: a bristling menace, a steamroller wearing a pair of boots, a player on a mission to help transform the mood – Enzo Le Fée’s decisive spot kick owed everything to Brobbey.

Chelsea arrived on Wearside looking to establish themselves in the top four ahead of the break but, instead, Alonso watched through his fingers as Sunderland reminded everyone why they were the joyous story of last season, a beautiful mix of inspiration and perspiration.

In fairness to the Chelsea manager, he refused to get caught in the minutiae of contentious penalty decisions – one that Chelsea were denied, another that they conceded – and could only lament as Sunderland ground out their first Premier League win since August 30, 70 long days ago.

“It wasn’t the best game,” Alonso said. “I think that we didn’t deserve more than probably one point, maybe. We need to be more consistent on the move, to get the ball from one side to the other, and we didn’t do that good enough. We didn’t produce enough to deserve to win.”

Unlike Sunderland. If you had turned up at the Stadium of Light without looking at the Premier League table, you would not have believed the hosts were bottom and you would not have given credence to the idea Le Bris, who has worked miracles these past two years, was under pressure.

Things, however, could not have started worse for Le Bris. Though Granit Xhaka has not shown last season’s form in these challenging opening months, the game plan was built around him, so to see the Sunderland captain hobbling off after three minutes was symptomatic of how things have gone for the Wearsiders.

“He felt something in the final sprint of the warm-up,” Le Bris explained. “We don’t know how bad it is.”

He is not the kind of coach, though, who will bemoan bad fortune. Le Bris sent on Jules Ahoka to replace Xhaka and watched as he, along with colleagues in red and white, set about trampling all over Chelsea’s intentions with incessant hard work.

Yet there was more to it. Sunderland can play, either intricately or directly, and a lovely move in the 12th minute needed a desperate, sliding intervention from Pep Chavarría’s to stop Trai Hume’s volley sliding in at the far post.

In the next attack, another Chemsdine Talbi cross – the Moroccan having been found by a peach of a pass from goalkeeper Robin Roefs – invited Brobbey to inflict maximum damage, but the Dutchman made a hash of his opportunity.

So close for Brobbey! 🤏 Sunderland almost take the lead against Chelsea. https://t.co/CUE6jHbPH2

The momentum could have changed completely in the 23rd minute. Alonso, his players and staff were convinced they would be given a penalty after Cole Palmer tumbled when his legs tangled with Luke O’Nien but, after a lengthy delay, VAR Nick Hopton felt there was no case to answer.

Hopton was involved again in the 33rd minute but, as Alonso said, Chelsea only had themselves to blame. Colwill simply could not contain Brobbey when he began marauding, grappling, grabbing and clipping the Dutchman’s heels. Le Fée did the rest, sending Mike Penders the wrong way.

Enzo Le Fee dispatches the penalty as Sunderland take the lead against Chelsea! 🔴⚪️ https://t.co/cCtYsHVWB9

From that point, Chelsea were in trouble, no matter how many changes Alonso made. They huffed, puffed, but nothing worked. They had come up against a red-and-white wall, fortified by constant backing from the stands, and the west Londoners were never going to knock it down.

One incident, as the clock ticked towards 90 minutes, encapsulated everything good about this Sunderland display when O’Nien chased down substitute Geovany Quenda to make a challenge. Another moment of defending from Thomas Meunier on Morgan Rogers was exceptional.

“You could see our identity and our togetherness and the way we managed the game,” said Le Bris, who was booked when hectoring referee Jarred Gillett. “These three points were critical. It was a struggle at times to manage situations. We showed as a group real heart.”

And nobody did that more than Brobbey. No wonder Le Bris will be hoping Xavi Hernández, the Netherlands head coach, handles him with care over the next 10 days. On this form, he will be the fuel that drives Sunderland’s quest for survival.

“You know when you come here in this stadium it will be a difficult game and that was the matter tonight. We knew it would be tough, we are disappointed we lost the game. At one point it went very fast from side to side. Sometimes we had to control. With 11 behind the ball it is difficult to find the spaces.”

On where Chelsea stand ahead of the international break...

“How you do – good or not – it is a matter of staying together. The international break is coming so the lads can be calm in the head and when we all come back we need to be motivated to go again.”

“For me it wasn’t a penalty. He barely touched him, I think it was the other way round. He grabbed him.”

They cannot make anything of set piece and Sunderland have the three points - it wasn’t pretty but they needed the three points and edged the contest.

Questions will be asked of Chelsea now, they were bullied in the first-half and weren’t able to create anything in the second.

Chelsea with the ball inside the Sunderland half. The visitors bring Rogers down and Chelsea have a free-kick. Last-chance sallon for the west Londoners...

Sunderland have a throw inside the Chelsea half - this is about game management for the side in dire need of a win now...

Angulo nrings down his man after a poor pass from Sadiki. The visitors with a free-kick inside their own half.

Emegha drifts past Mukiele before he feels the full force of a Luke O’Nein tackle. It looks as though he gets the ball but the ref awards the free-kick. It’s in the final third, can Chelsea create anything from this?

In short ‘yes’, Estevao delivers a peach of a ball and Welbeck gets on the end of it. BUT his header is over, when it seemed easier to hit the target.

Sunderland in Chelsea half, they’re looking for a free-kick as Angulo goes down. The referee isn’t having any of it...

Sunderland break at pace (only the second time this half) Isador finds Talbi who is free before cutting inside and unleashing a shot from outside the box. It’s just wide, don’t think it was too far away though.

Talbi is off for Angulo, Rigg on for Le Fee for Sunderland, and for Chelsea, Henderson makes way for Emegha.

For all their possession this half Chelsea have not forced Roefs into a meaningful save. The west Londoners are again dominating possession in and near the hinterland of the Sunderland box, but it’s all a bit after you Claude and ultimately Roefs gladly picks up an anaemic cross. That sums up Chelsea as an attacking force today.

Chelsea corner after Geovany Quenda gets in a shot from the left-side of the area that gets a tiny hint of a deflection. Roefs punches away the set-piece and Sunderland breathe a sigh of relief.

Better from Sunderland, there are spaces in behind Chelsea as the visitors go in search of the equaliser and over the past few minutes the hosts have found them.

Lovely ball from Reinildo finds Sadiki in space on the left, they keep the ball brilliantly before Le Fee plays in Isador, it’s a one-on-one and all the Frenchman has to do it dink it over the on-rushing keeper. He goes low, however, and Penders makes a fine save - that was the game for Sunderland there...Penders has kept Chelsea in this.

Brobbey may have been tiring but without him Sunderland cannot keep the ball. Sadiki earns a free-kick which takes a bit of pressure off the hosts.

Palmer pulls back for Gusto whose dinky, cheeky chip tries to find Roefs off his line. He doesn’t succeed and the Dutch goalkeeper claims with ease.

Chelsea still seeing plenty of the ball, Sunderland may well be tiring. It’s hard to keep up that intensity for 90 minutes, hence Isador on for Brobbey, but they are struggling to keep the ball at the moment.

The first half was lively and entertaining, this half has been lively and lacking in anything that could be remotely described as a spectacle...

Rogers tries to find Palmer, but the ball is too long and Roefs gobbles up with ease.

Meanwhile, Hume looks injured and Chelsea do not give the ball back after Sunderland kicked it off. You won’t be shocked to hear that the home fans are not happy with that...

Change for Sunderland, Brobbey off for Isador. The Dutchman has been brilliant today, he might have scored a couple of goals, but despite not finding the back of the net he has proved a handful for the Chelsea backline. I would have kept him on for longer...

Chelsea looking better this half, they’re seeing plenty of the ball but have not had a shot on goal since the break. In fact there have only been two touches in either box this 45...Sunderland won’t mind that at 1-0.

ON - Welbeck and GustoOFF - Neto and Palestra

So Alonso has opted for a physical presence up front.

No sooner had I pressed send on that last post than Chelsea break through the middle but some great last-ditch defending from Muenier prevents Estevao from getting a shot at goal.

Chelsea haven’t been able to play through Sunderland and you think they’d need to bring on a physical presence up front if that’s to change.

Another chance for Sunderland - they break down the right before Hume sends in a low ball to the penalty box, it’s met first time by Le Fee, I think, and Penders saves low to his right. To state the obvious, the hosts would love a second to give them a deserved cushion. As I typed that last but the linesman has his flag up, it wouldn’t have counted, promising signs nonetheless.

Pressure from Sunderland. A good bit of possession ends with Mukiele swinging in a lovely cross from the right which Chelsea are forced to head clear for a corner. Nothing results from the set piece, but things still looking promising for Sunderland who look as energetic and ‘at it’ as they did in the first half.

Rogers picks up the ball in the middle just inside the Sunderland half and is immediately pick-pocketed by one of three Sunderland players. The Chelsea men have not been allowed to settle when they have a sniff of a mini counter.

Good, feisty opening to this half, Chelsea look more up for it, though to be fair they couldn’t look any more insipid than they did in the first 45. Meanwhile, Brobbey shoves Lavia and earns a yellow. Think that’s three yellows for the hosts now.

It is going to be fascinating to see how a team with well known - and long standing - disciplinary issues copes with a pressurised pursuit of an equaliser. There have already been a couple of flash points that Chelsea’s players have reacted to and it wouldn’t be the wildest thing to predict referee Jarred Gillett brandishing a red card before the end of the game. Watch it unfold with interest.

Brobbey lays the ball off for Meunier in the final third, it’s asking a lot of the Belgian but his compounds the Dutchman’s error with one of his own - stretching for the ball and taking out Caicedo. Something for which he earns a needless yellow card.

There’s a bit of argy bargy on the pitch, not sure what started that but the referee Jarred Gillett has to have a word with several players. All a bit of handbags really.

They’re back under way on the banks of the Wear. Chelsea have been insipid and you imagine they won’t be as bed these next 45 minutes. Can Sunderland play with the same aggression and energy? We’re about to find out.

Changes Estevao on for Colwill, interesting substitution to say the least...

So close for Brobbey! 🤏 Sunderland almost take the lead against Chelsea. https://t.co/CUE6jHbPH2

The half ends with an audacious attempt at goal from Rogers, a full 40 yards out from a free kick. It’s catching practice for Roefs and that sums up Chelsea as an attacking force in the first 45. Sunderland are well worth their lead.

Rogers has a shot-cum-cross from the left and it sails high, wide and not so handsome. He’s been on the periphery this half, as has Palmer and that explains as much as anything why they are behind. Sunderland have cut out the supply to him and Roefs has had little to do as a result.

Approaching half-time and save for the contentious VAR call when he wanted a penalty, Cole Palmer has done absolutely nothing. The talk of him being in the England squad, on this evidence, is for the birds. Sunderland are full value for their half-time lead. Chelsea, like Palmer, have been absolutely insipid.

There will be five minutes added time in this first half.

Something I’ve not written much this half ‘chance for Chelsea’. Neto works a bit of space in the inside-right channel outside the box, but his shot is easily saved by Roefs.

Talbi attacks down the left but cuts in when he would have been better served going wide.

Chelsea have seen plenty of the ball but they’ve been way too slow and cumbersome with it. It’s been in front of the Sunderland back lines and easy to defend against. The hosts are letting the visitors have the ball wide and with Neto in the middle, it’s been too easy for Le Bris’s men.

Brobbey wants the ball at every opportunity and Sunderland would be well advised to give it to him. Colwill is has his hands full.

Sunderland have kept the aggression and energy throughout the half - and kept Chelsea quiet as a result. As I type that the hosts give Lavia too much room 25 yards out and his shot is well wide of the left-hand post.

The lead is no more than Sunderland deserve and that means, as the table stands, Manchester United are bottom of the Premier League. Fair play to Enzo Le Fee for keeping his nerve in a pressure situation. Sunderland needed him to be cool.

They’ve deserved that, they’ve been the better side and are well worth the lead. Le Fee sends Penders the wrong way, burying the ball into the bottom left corner.

Brobbey has been a handful (as he always is) and Colwill brings the BIG (yes, caps lock and bold are necessary) Dutchman down in the box. It looks as though it was six of one and hald a dozen of the other, but the spotkick stands.

Ahoka has impressed since coming on, his nifty footwork helps win Sunderland a throw in the final third. Mukiele has a big thrown on him but it does not result in a chance. Still, this is good from the hosts and Chelsea are second best at the moment. They were in the first half against United last week, and ended up winning so...

Another chance for Sunderland as Brobbey bullies Colwill on the halfway line before driving at Fofana. He gets to the edge of the area, beats the Chelsea defender before his shot goes wide. The last touch took him too wide, but again, promising signs for the hosts.

Early days this, of course, but Sunderland absolutely do not look like a team that is currently the worst in the Premier League. They should have the lead here but Brian Brobbey’s miss from six yards is indicative of how things have been going.

Sunderland are being aggressive, they need to be and it’s a contrast from the previous month. With that approach, however, comes risks and Mukiele gives away a free-kick inside his own half. Luckily for him, nothing comes from the set-piece.

First chance of the game for Chelsea and, as with Brobbey 10 minutes ago, it should have found the back of the net. Rogers is the culprit - he sends his header wide of the right post after a grade-A cross from Palestra.

One-all in terms of great chances...but the score remains 0-0.

Palmer is bundled over on the outskirts of the area and he and Chelsea players appeal for something - could be a free-kick of penalty...the referee is having nothing of it. The replay suggests he may well have been hard done by but VAR also is having nothing of it...it was a foul as none of the marauding Sunderland players, O’Nien among them (obviously), got the ball and most definitely got Palmer...think the hosts got away with that one.

Yellow card for Ahoka for a foul on Caicado, he may need to walk a tightrope for the rest of the match. But it’s an illustration of the energy and purpose with which Sunderland have approached this match.

Sunderland have looked the better side so far and have had the better chances.

Better from Chelsea in the sense that they controlled the game for two minutes. Lots of good, neat passing but no end product, it’s all in front of a composed Sunderland defence.

Another good chance for Sunderland and once again Talbi proves his worth. He cuts back onto his right and delivers a peach of a cross from the left. Brobbey gets in front of his man and all he has to do is hit the target...alas his first-time shot goes wide. That should be 1-0 to the hosts who are the better side at the moment.

Good from Sunderland who look so much more energetic than at any point during their previous few matches. Ahoka does well in the middle before freeing Talbi down the left. The Moroccan gets in a cross and Le Fee’s shot is blocked. Promising signs for the hosts.

What a blow this is for Regis Le Bris. Less than two minutes gone and Granit Xhaka is having to leave the pitch with an obvious injury. Some fans around the press box booed Xhaka as he was hobbling off - is that a hangover from his attempts to move to Chelsea? - but on afternoon when Le Bris needed everything to go his way, he’s already on the back foot.

Neto is in the Sunderland half but three Sunderland players snap at his heels like a hyperactive dog after a bone. Chelsea haven’t been allowed to settle yet. Plenty of time to go though...

Sunderland are looking to find Brobbey at every opportunity, but Chelsea’s backline intercept well. Nothing of note created so far, but the hosts are on the front foot, which is what they and the fans needed.

Sunderland attack down the right with Meunier, nothing comes of it but the hosts look as though they mean business here. A minute later Sadiki and Brobbey nearly combine to create something. Close but no cigar...

Bad news for Sunderland, Xhaka is down and it looks as though he may well have to come off...oh dear. While he’s not been at his best this season he’s still the man the side looks towards for inspiration (an boy do they need that is dollops today...)...and, indeed he is forced off. Ahoka, who is highly rated but raw replaces him. The Congolese player now has a big chance to make a name for himself.

Chelsea with the early possession, but they go backwards and the hosts are up and at them with the press and the visitors have to go back to Penders in goal.

They’re under way at the Stadium of Light, Sunderland are in their famous red and white and Chelsea in their away outfit of black shirts and shorts and yelow socks.

As the Stadium of Light remembers all those who lost their lives in war.

The Last Post is played and the minute’s silence is impeccably observed.

Warming-up in our Remembrance shirt ❤️ https://t.co/aTB8sfdLKP

And we’re moments away from kick-off in the North East.

#985. Hashim Thaci's second conviction in The Hague reignites debate in Kosovo about justice and the Kosovo Specialist Chambers

Former President Hashim Thaci has been convicted of trying to influence witnesses in his war crimes trial. The conviction has reignited debate in Kosovo about the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, the court that convicted him.

A court in The Hague on Tuesday convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci of obstructing justice and attempting to influence witnesses during his recent war crimes trial and sentenced him to 17 months in prison.

This term will be added to his 25-year sentence for war crimes, which was handed down by the same court, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, on September 16.

According to the indictment of the Specialist Prosecutor's Office, Thaci had provided visitors at the detention facility in The Hague with confidential information about witnesses in his war crimes trial and had instructed them on how to influence their testimony.

Three other men — former head of the Kosovo Intelligence Agency Bashkim Smakaj, former Minister of Justice Hajredin Kuci, and Fadil Fazliu — were also convicted.

Thaci, who was the former political leader of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) during the 1998-1999 Kosovo War, is viewed by many in his home country as a hero. His war crimes conviction in September was greeted in Kosovo with anger and dismay.

Thaci has vowed to appeal the war crimes conviction.

His two convictions touch deep sensitivities in Kosovo society. Tuesday's ruling brings renewed attention to the war that ended 27 years ago, the role played by its former leaders, and the continuing debate over justice, individual or collective responsibility for the KLA's war to liberate Kosovo from Serbia, and trust in judicial institutions.

The response from the government of Kosovo was swift.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, the government said, "Trust in justice is built not only on the decisions that are made, but also on the manner in which they are reached. Therefore, our commitment to the rule of law and our insistence on the full respect of rights and procedural guarantees are part of the same principled position: Justice must not only be done, but must also be fair, transparent, and credible."

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was established in 2015 by the parliament of Kosovo at the instigation of the European Union and the United States.

The court was created to investigate serious crimes allegedly committed by members of the KLA during and after the Kosovo War.

For security reasons, including concerns about witness intimidation, the court was located in The Hague in the Netherlands.

After Thaci and three others were convicted of war crimes in first instance in September, Kosovo's state authorities established a working group to draft a strategy regarding the appeal proceedings before the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The group is chaired by Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca and includes members of Kosovo's parliament.

Prime Minister Albin Kurti has stated that the working group continues to believe that "the first-instance judgment of the Specialist Chambers is unjust, both legally and morally," and that as a result, "the government is working to secure a correction at the appeals level before the Specialist Chambers."

In addition, the parliament of Kosovo is currently considering amendments to the law governing the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The draft law, which is expected to be adopted, envisages narrowing the court's mandate in several areas, including the time period covered by its jurisdiction, limiting the maximum prison sentence to 15 years, allowing sentences to be served in Kosovo, and introducing the possibility of presidential pardons for persons convicted by final court decisions.

How do political analysts and legal experts view the parliament's attempt to amend the law on the Kosovo Specialist Chambers before the judicial process involving the four men convicted of war crimes has reached a final verdict?

"From an international perspective, at first glance, this initiative could even be interpreted as an attempt to interfere in the judicial process," said political analyst and university professor Artan Muhaxheri.

"Precisely for this reason, it is essential that Kosovo's political spectrum and its legal experts demonstrate beyond any doubt that this measure does not conflict with Kosovo's international obligations toward the European Union," Muhaxheri told DW, adding that this is the only way to ensure that the desired outcome is achieved and that the initiative does not produce the opposite effect.

"Issues relating to jurisdiction, statutory limits on maximum sentences, and other similar matters must be argued professionally and rigorously, demonstrating that they fully guarantee judicial independence and enjoy solid support within Kosovo's legal system, the same legal system that, first and foremost, established the Specialist Chambers," he said.

Ehat Miftaraj, executive director of the Kosovo Law Institute (IKD), told DW that although the Kosovo Specialist Chambers were established by the Republic of Kosovo itself, "the way the judicial process has unfolded has created the impression that judges, prosecutors and certain international actors have treated not only the accused but also Kosovo itself with distrust, prejudice, and an often condescending approach."

Miftaraj went on to say that reactions and objections in Kosovo to the decisions of the Specialist Chambers are also interpreted and judged in the historical and emotional context of the war and what Kosovo's citizens experienced during and after it.

"In a democratic society, every citizen, including political and institutional representatives, has the right to criticize judicial decisions," he said. "However, there is a fundamental distinction between criticism based on legal arguments and attempts to delegitimize courts or exert influence over judicial proceedings. And here, there is room for criticism of both sides."

#980. Can smart cities attract the talent they need to thrive?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Robots compete in a football event during RoboCup 2026, a robotics and AI competition held at the Songdo Convensia convention centre in Incheon, South Korea. Credit: Ahn Young-joon/Associated Press/ALAMY

More than half of the world’s population now lives in cities, and that figure is projected to increase to nearly 70% by 2050. With the numbers of urban dwellers set to expand rapidly in some regions, a new generation of towns and cities is on the rise: communities that are designed to be cleaner and more efficient, driven by a host of technologies such as artificial intelligence and the Internet of Things — a network of sensors and devices that collect and transmit data about their surroundings.

As the global competition for talent and investment intensifies, many governments see these new cities and urban areas as strategic resources for boosting their innovative and economic competitiveness. Research facilities, both public and private, are central to this strategy.

In Songdo, South Korea — an early experiment in building a smart city from the ground up — biopharmaceutical giants such as Samsung Biologics have built major manufacturing facilities, and academic institutions such as Yonsei University have set up training and research centres to nurture scientists. In Hengqin, a rapidly developing district in the Pearl River Delta of southern China, research institutions also play a key role in a government strategy aimed at attracting talent, diversifying the economy and building a reputation for high-tech innovation.

For some researchers, purpose-built tech-centric cities provide them with the ideal environment to conduct experiments. Air-quality and traffic-flow research benefits greatly from consistent, real-time data gathered from many different locations, for instance. “Smart cities can offer something very valuable: a real-world laboratory,” says Dakota McCarty, a researcher of urban planning at George Mason University’s Songdo campus.

But building a liveable city from scratch takes more than implementing advanced technologies and creating favourable conditions for institutions. Many large-scale urban projects across the world are facing a collective challenge: how to convince talented people to live there?

The term ‘smart cities’ generally refers to places that are made to run more efficiently and sustainably through the extensive use of digital technologies. Songdo, located about 40 kilometres southwest of South Korea’s capital, Seoul, is often described as “the world’s first smart city”1. The idea for Songdo dates back to the 1980s, but construction did not begin until several years after the 1998 Asian financial crisis, when the Incheon metropolitan government proposed developing Songdo as part of a free economic zone aimed at attracting foreign investment2. Today, Songdo spans about 5,260 hectares of coastal land, roughly the size of Manhattan.

In 2011, a series of futuristic technologies was built into Songdo’s infrastructure as part of South Korea’s campaign to establish ‘ubiquitous cities’, its name for smart cities at the time. One example is its underground waste-collection system — a network of subterranean pipes that suck rubbish directly from individual households, rather than transporting it by road. The system uses bins fitted with sensors and built into the stairwells of residential buildings. Once the sensors detect that the bins are full, the system will automatically empty them and send the rubbish through the pipes to a waste centre. Recyclable rubbish is cleaned and reused, and food waste is processed into compost.

In addition to the use of sensors in waste disposal, Songdo has deployed thousands of sensors to help manage other city functions such as traffic and security. These sensor networks link to a control centre run by the Incheon Free Economic Zone Authority (IFEZA), which manages Songdo and two other free economic zones in Incheon.

Extensive sensor networks and integrated data systems are a major asset for Songdo’s researchers and students, says McCarty, who moved from the United States to South Korea nearly a decade ago and has spent the past three years in Songdo. “In a place like Songdo, which was planned from the start with smart infrastructure, and has universities, industry and public agencies relatively close together, there is much more potential to test ideas in real urban conditions,” he says.

Data can be accessed through a website run by IFEZA, with additional data sets available on request. McCarty and his students are combining traffic data obtained from IFEZA with observations collected on the ground to build a model of Songdo’s walkability. The team hopes to show that adjusting traffic-light timings could make the city more accommodating for pedestrians without increasing congestion3.

There is a downside to building a city’s renown around cutting-edge technology, however: other cities can catch up. As the novelty of Songdo’s original smart-city infrastructure started to fade, it increasingly sought to build its identity around industry clusters that are harder for competitors to replicate.

Biopharmaceuticals, for example, is a strategic industry for South Korea, with the government committing US$1.5 billion to support the sector over this decade. Celltrion, one of South Korea’s largest biotechnology companies, was among the first firms of its kind to commit to Songdo in 2003. Samsung Biologics, a major biopharmaceutical manufacturer, established its headquarters there in 2011.

Moves like this helped to create a new development path for the city, says Sohyun Park, a researcher of economic geography at George Mason University in Songdo. “As these firms expanded, local and national governments increasingly concentrated resources on developing Songdo as a biotechnology cluster,” says Park. As of 2021, Songdo was home to around 60 biotechnology companies, and the government’s plan is to expand that number to 700 by 2030.

Dakota McCarty and his team at George Mason University’s Songdo campus are using traffic data to come up with ways to make the city more pedestrian-friendly.Credit: Dakota McCarty / George Mason University Korea

Such expansion depends on the support of Songdo’s university sector to train a new generation of biomedical talent. Yonsei University, which has its main campus in Seoul and an international campus in Songdo, opened the Korean National Institute for Bioprocessing Research and Training (K-NIBRT) in Songdo last year. The project has received around 60.9 billion South Korean won (US$41 million) from national and regional authorities and aims to train 2,000 biopharmaceutical specialists each year to address labour shortages locally and across the country.

K-NIBRT benefits from Songdo’s complete biopharmaceuticals value chain, says Gyoonhee Han, the institution’s director-general, because its research institutes, drug manufacturers and raw material and equipment suppliers are all conveniently packed into a radius of a 10-minute drive. This tight-knit ecosystem means that companies, researchers and academics can collaborate efficiently where industry is located, and trainees are able to enter the workforce as soon as they graduate, says Han.

Beyond biopharmaceuticals, Songdo plans on expanding its university base more broadly, particularly within its Incheon Global Campus (IGC), a higher-education zone established in the early 2010s and backed by US$1 billion in investment from the Korean and Incheon Metropolitan City governments. Campuses of three US universities — George Mason University, the University of Utah and the State University of New York (which has two Songdo campuses) — plus Belgium’s Ghent University have opened in the IGC, and six more universities are expected to join in the coming years.

Songdo’s evolution reflects a broader challenge for smart-city projects: advanced technologies and digital infrastructure can attract investment and attention, but long-term R&D activity depends on assets that are harder to build: universities, skilled workforces and specialized industry clusters.

In Hengqin, an island in southern China’s Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA), regional and central governments are trying to combine both approaches. In addition to the autonomous-vehicle technologies that Hengqin and the wider GBA area are known for — including driverless buses, taxis and delivery services — universities and research institutes are being positioned at the centre of Hengqin’s development strategy.

Hengqin entered a new phase of cross-border cooperation in 2009, when China’s central government passed legislation enabling Macau, a special administrative region with its own governance system, to exercise jurisdiction over part of the neighbouring island. The goal was to allow the University of Macau to move its campus away from a densely populated casino hub, and more broadly to have Hengqin serve as a bridge between Macau and the neighbouring Guangdong province.

These efforts were accelerated in 2021, when China established the Guangdong–Macao In-Depth Cooperation Zone — an economic and administrative area covering more than 100 km2 of Hengqin, run jointly by the Macau and Guangdong governments. One of the biggest projects within this new zone is an international university town, expected to be completed by 2030 at a cost of nearly 20 billion Macau pataca (US$2.47 billion). At least three universities plan to open campuses there — the University of Macau (which will build an additional campus alongside an existing one), Macao Polytech University and Macao University of Tourism — to accommodate roughly 20,000 students.

Students develop flexible electronics in the Soft Sensors-Actuators-Robots Laboratory at the University of Macau’s main campus in Hengqin.Credit: The University of Macau

“Academic and research capabilities are essential, because they provide the talent, knowledge and innovation infrastructure that Hengqin needs to become a science and technology hub,” says Yonghua Song, president of the Macao Association for Higher Education Development and rector of the University of Macau. Song adds that new facilities such as the University of Macau’s Faculty of Information Science and Computing, opened in August, are expected to train talent in highly competitive areas such as artificial intelligence, microelectronics and financial technology.

Like Songdo, researchers in Hengqin benefit from its extensive smart-city infrastructure, including the large networks of sensors in operation across the island. According to Ma Shaodan, a wireless-communications researcher at the University of Macau’s State Key Laboratory of Internet of Things for Smart City in Hengqin, having smart-city infrastructure right outside the laboratory removes many of the constraints of conventional research environments. “It provides an invaluable physical context that accelerates our research, strengthens our regional impact, and serves as a tangible blueprint to inspire the next generation of engineers,” she says.

Early signs suggest that Hengqin’s strategy to become a place of high-tech innovation is gaining momentum: the University of Macau has expanded its presence, research infrastructure has proliferated and authorities continue to invest heavily in the cooperation zone.

#978. Man Utd are in relegation trouble and Carrick must be sacked

Michael Carrick stood perfectly still and raised his left arm, and his index finger, high in the air. Around him, chaos. As it had been all afternoon. Substitute Patrick Dorgu had just headed in a corner to rescue a point for Manchester United in the 96th minute and, maybe, save Carrick his job.

Going into added time and United were two goals behind. It seemed all was lost for them against Aston Villa and for their head coach, but how telling was the reaction, in the directors’ box, of chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox, who both jumped up in celebration? They were far more animated than Carrick and could not contain themselves.

"Football is a contact sport!" 🗣️ Did Senne Lammens foul Zion Suzuki for Man United's equaliser? 🤔 https://t.co/KCb1lHqPHP

Did their behaviour betray not just their excitement in the moment but their relief at not having to sack Carrick during this forthcoming international break? If so, they need to think again. They need to make a sober and rational decision based on evidence. And the evidence shows that Carrick must go. Because this kind of football is unsustainable. This kind of football does not work. This kind of football is stupid.

United are 18th in the Premier League. They have won one game in 10 in the league. They have conceded 15 goals in their last five matches in the league and Champions League. When they play Liverpool away, their next game, on November 22, it will be the first time they have done so from inside the relegation zone since March 1937.

They appear shockingly disorganised. Tactics seem to be an after-thought, their motivation is lacking until desperation kicks in. United conceded two goals within four minutes at the start of the game. And then two more within eight minutes of the second half kicking off.

The bottom line is this: can they afford not to make a change? If they do not, United could be accused of copping out and gambling with their status. So, Berrada and Wilcox must ask: what is Carrick doing in the dressing room and on the training ground? What messages are he and his assistant Steve Holland sending out? Are the players even listening?

At the end the fans sang Carrick’s name after United became the first team in the Premier League to come back twice from being two goals down. That also summed up the fog of confusion at a club who so obviously lack direction – from the top down – and need to get a grip of themselves. Carrick talked about having to “tighten up” the defending. But everything needs to be stronger. More taut. More competitive.

Chaos can be entertaining. Chaos can be fun. As an advert for the Premier League this was outstanding. United fans will be thrilled with the Fergie-time comeback. But chaos is also unsustainable. No one knows what to expect from United.

In the cold light of day Villa manager Unai Emery will have to ask himself whether he, too, got it wrong. His substitutions did not work, bizarrely taking off too much experience, such as his outstanding captain John McGinn, and he handed United a late initiative when it looked like all hope was lost.

But analyse the goals that United conceded. Any rational response would suggest a change should be made. Take the first two. Villa scored with their first attack, moving the ball from a throw-in, with zero pressure on them, from left to right with McGinn finding Alysson. The winger’s low first-time shot went through the legs of goalkeeper Senne Lammens, who had an awful game. Lammens’s only positive contribution was to come up for the late corner from which Dorgu scored, possibly getting away with a sly nudge on Villa’s Zion Suzuki.

What a start for Aston Villa! 🔥 Alysson fires home to give the the visitors the lead https://t.co/F0nfSRMWRa

Then Lammens conceded a second as he fumbled a shot from Alysson, after the Brazilian was again teed up by McGinn with Nicolas Jackson tucking home the rebound. It followed a poor defensive header from Leny Yoro. It would not be his last one.

Nicolas Jackson has made it 2-0 to Aston Villa after just 4 minutes and boos ring out around Old Trafford 🤯 https://t.co/G7oWDNMjGS

At that point, even so early, it felt over. For United. For Carrick. Then it got complicated. In fairness, United responded brilliantly. By half-time it was 2-2 and a potentially mutinous situation, with the fans on edge and unfurling new banners attacking the hierarchy – including one which read “your funeral not ours” – had turned and were raucous in a positive way.

Matheus Cunha, with a sharp turn and run into the Villa penalty area before being brought down, earned the spot kick from which Bruno Fernandes pulled back the first goal. Former Villa midfielder Youri Tielemans drew them level with a first-time shot. Not just that but they peppered the Villa goal.

Youri Tielemans against his former club! 😱 Manchester United are level just before the break! https://t.co/8kFOQkl814

Then they conceded two more in quick succession with a ridiculous trip on Alysson by Diogo Dalot, who was given the runaround at left-back until he was substituted to cheers. McGinn scored from the penalty. It was 4-2 when Yoro inexplicably headed a McGinn free-kick goalwards, Lammens tipped it on to the crossbar and Leon Goretzka eventually bundled the ball in.

Tellingly, the United supporters appeared too stunned to protest. The game meandered to what felt like an inevitable conclusion, petering out much like, surely, Carrick’s time in charge.

But, football, bloody hell. As someone – who was appointed United manager 40 years ago last week – once said. Dorgu made a difference. As did Joshua Zirkzee, another substitute, as the pair became United’s unlikely saviours, the striker sweeping home the full-back’s cross in the 92nd minute, with six added on.

Then a corner was won. The roar went up – as did Lammens. But it was Dorgu who met the delivery from close range to salvage a point. But the big question is: did he also salvage Carrick?

Michael Carrick has insisted he remains the right man to lead Manchester United and will not walk away despite the club being marooned in the relegation zone.

United came from 2-0 and 4-2 down to claim a last-gasp 4-4 draw against Aston Villa on another wild day at Old Trafford.It means United still only have one Premier League win to their name this season and are languishing in 18th position, a point adrift of safety, heading into the international break when the Old Trafford hierarchy must decide whether to keep faith with Carrick or appoint their third manager this year.

Carrick cut a spiky figure when asked about his future by Sky Sports and whether he would walk away.

“That’s not going to happen,” Carrick said, before asking “will there?” when it was put to him that there would “clearly” be conversations about his future.

“We haven’t won enough games, but I expect to move forward and keep working on the things we’ve been working on and showing a lot of good in the game today,” he said. “Tighten up on some things and start winning football matches.”

"That's not going to happen" 🗣️ Michael Carrick responds to the notion that he could resign as Manchester United head coach 🔴 https://t.co/q1fBKSXL7l

Asked later if he had seen enough to turn the situation around, the United head coach added: “Yeah, 100 per cent. I think there’s more than enough. Goals change games and you’ve got to deal with it, and it’s part of something we have to improve on drastically, but there’s more than enough.”Carrick scoffed at talk of United being in a relegation battle. “We’re in November,” he said. “I don’t like this situation where we are and where we’re at. But we can do something about it.”

Roy Keane, the former United captain, likened Carrick to a “politician”. “It’s hard to believe what’s coming out of the United camp because we can’t even be sure they’re being honest with themselves. It’s just words,” he said. “It’s obviously difficult for the manager. Under pressure, no doubt. He talks a lot but doesn’t say much. I don’t know if that’s a tactic. Like a politician.

“He keeps saying we need to tighten up and there’s things we need to work on. But they better get moving on that.”

Manchester United will spend the international break in the relegation zone and are winless in their last eight Premier League games, but it could have been so much worse.

The game looked over when six minutes of stoppage time were indicated, but Joshua Zirkzee’s goal changed the atmosphere and then Zion Suzuki was found wanting from a corner and Patrick Dorgu equalised.

Nobody in Old Trafford knows what to think, apart from Villa fans who must devastated that they chucked it away. Twice.

The question now is whether United showed enough to spare Carrick the sack.

The game has just restarted with 98 minutes on the clock.

And United are on the attack again through Fernandes, who feeds Mount on the left but his low cross is in front of everyone.

With Lammens up for the corner, Suzuki makes a mess of it in the six-yard box and grasps fresh air, allowing Dorgu to nod home an improbable equaliser. Villa will be sick, they have thrown this away.

Emery marches straight down the tunnel. How important will that be for Carrick? Answers on a postcard.
